input: It is important to note that the performance of a vapour-compression unit serving a process chiller can be looked at from several complementary angles, and each angle contributes something to a fuller understanding of the machine. On the temperature side, the unit evaporates at 0 °C and condenses at 45 °C, which sets the thermal stage on which everything else plays out. Against this background, the Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures is 6.07, representing the idealised benchmark that no real refrigerator operating between the same temperatures can exceed. The installed unit, by contrast, achieves 2.3, a figure that comes from the manufacturer's test at full load and therefore reflects the machine as actually built and tested rather than as ideally conceived. It is also worth bearing in mind that part-load performance is not stated, so the picture that emerges is essentially a full-load picture, and any broader generalisation about how the unit behaves across its whole operating envelope would go beyond what the available information can support. This distinction between the ideal and the achieved is, in many ways, the central theme of practical refrigeration engineering. Taken together, these points suggest a machine whose tested performance sits well below the reversible benchmark, with the part-load region remaining, for the moment, uncharacterised.
target: The installed unit achieves a coefficient of performance of 2.3 at full load. Between the same temperatures, the Carnot coefficient of performance is 6.07. The machine is a vapour-compression unit serving a process chiller, evaporating at 0 °C and condensing at 45 °C. A coefficient of performance states the refrigeration effect obtained for each unit of work supplied, so the two values are compared on the same basis. The Carnot value is the reversible limit for refrigeration between those temperatures, and the achieved value comes from the manufacturer's test at full load. Part-load performance is not stated. The achieved coefficient of performance is therefore a full-load figure, and it carries no information about operation at reduced load, where a process chiller may spend much of its running time. No part-load test result stands behind any extension of the figure. The distance between the two values is the aggregate effect of the irreversibilities in the real machine, and the brief assigns no share of that distance to the compressor, the expansion device, or the heat exchangers. Any comparison with another unit is sound only at the tested condition: same duty point, same temperature levels, and a measured rather than estimated achieved value. Stated at its tested scope, the result is a full-load coefficient of performance below the reversible limit, with part-load behaviour unstated.
